13-073.r: Lifeline of the Pandya state → Vaigai/Vengi river (rises near Madurai); Pandya kingdom covered Madurai and Tirunelveli; capital Madura.
13-073.t: Don't pick Godavari, Krishna or Tungabhadra; those are Deccan rivers, far north of Pandya land.
13-073.c: The Pandya river meant is the Vaigai of Madurai; option (d) 'Vengi' stands for it. Vengi is really a region in Andhra between the Krishna and Godavari, not a river.

13-074.r: Sangam ports on the western coast → Tondi and Mushiri (also Naura, Nelisanda), per the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea; Korkai and Puhar are not western.

13-075.r: Korkai, Poompuhar and Muchiri → ports; Korkai = Pandya port; Poompuhar (Kaveripattinam) = early Chola capital-port; Muziris/Muchiri = Kerala port.
13-075.h: Korkai-Pandya, Puhar-Chola, Muchiri-Chera: three Sangam kingdoms, three ports.

13-076.r: Sangam texts: Kon, Ko and Mannan → titles of the King.

13-077.r: Third Sangam → Madurai; all three Sangams held under Pandya patronage; 1st at Madurai (Saint Agastya), 2nd at Kapadapuram.

13-078.r: Sage who Aryanised South India → Agastya; also called 'Father of Tamil Literature'.

13-079.r: Capitals: Chalukyas → Badami; Pallavas → Kanchipuram; Harsha → Kannauj; Pandyas → Madurai.

13-080.r: Mahendravarman I → Pallava; Kadungon → Pandya; Amoghavarsha I → Rashtrakuta; Rajaraja I → Chola.

13-081.r: Order: Pallava power under Mahendravarman I (600-630 AD) → Pala dynasty by Gopala (750) → Pratihara Bhoja (836-885) → Chola Parantaka I (907-953).
13-081.h: South-East-North-South: Pallava, Pala, Pratihara, then Chola.

13-082.r: Wrong pair: Chera–Puducheri; Chera capital was Vanchi. Correct: Pallava–Kanchipuram, Pandya–Madurai, Chola–Tanjavur, Hoysala–Dwarasamudra.

13-083.r: Chera capital → Karur/Karuvur (also called Vanchi; some sources say Thondi); Cheras ruled present Kerala and parts of Tamil Nadu.
13-083.t: Don't confuse with Kanchipuram (Pallava) or Madurai (Pandya).

13-084.r: Pallava order: Mahendravarman I (600-630) → Narasimhavarman I (630-668) → Parameshvaravarman I (c. 670-700) → Nandivarman II (731-795).

13-085.r: Titles Mattavilasa, Vichitrachitta and Gunabhara → Pallava king Mahendravarman I (c. 600–630 CE); titles found in Mandagapattu rock-cut temple inscription.

13-086.r: Chinese traveller who described China–India relations under the Chalukyas → Matwalin.
13-086.t: Don't pick Fa-Hien (Gupta age) or Hiuen-Tsang (Harsha); the Chalukya-era account is Matwalin's.

13-087.r: Chalukyas did not rule North India; ruled Deccan and South, capital Badami (Vatapi); Pulakesin II defeated Harshavardhana (618 AD); Chalukyas of Kalyani a later branch.

13-088.r: Chalukya king Kumarapala (Jain, disciple of Hemachandra; ruled 29 years) → sent ministers to stop cruelty to animals in Kashi region.

13-089.r: Kadamba capital → Banavasi (Vanavasi); founder Mayurasharman; annexed by Pulakesin II. Tanjore–Chola, Kanchi–Pallava, Badami–Chalukya.
13-089.h: Mayura (peacock) flew to the Vana (forest) → Banavasi.

13-090.r: Chief seaport of the Kakatiya kingdom → Motupalli; Marco Polo entered the Kakatiya land through it.

13-091.r: South Indian king who sent an ambassador to Rome in 26 B.C. → Pandya; longest-ruling South Indian dynasty, capital Madurai.

13-092.r: Trade with the Roman empire began with the Cheras (Sangam period); Roman objects found at Arikamedu (Puducherry).

13-093.r: Meenakshi temple → Madurai, Pandya capital; 1st and 3rd Sangam held here, presided by Agastya and Nakkirar.

13-095.r: Meenakshi Mandir → Madurai; Venkateswara Mandir → Tirumala (Andhra Pradesh); Mahakal Mandir → Ujjain; Belur Math → Howrah (Ramakrishna Mission HQ).

13-096.r: Huge gateways of South Indian temples → Gopurams; Dravidian style flourished under the Pandyas and Cholas.
13-096.t: Don't confuse Gopuram (gateway) with Shikhara (tower over sanctum) or Mandapam (pillared hall).

14-001.r: 'Father of History' → Herodotus (Greek); his 'Historica/The Histories' describes Indo-Persian relations in the 5th century B.C.

14-002.r: Ashtadhyayi → Panini; Mahabhashya → Patanjali; Nirukta → Yaska; Varttika → Katyayan.
14-002.h: Panini wrote the rules, Katyayan added notes (Varttika), Patanjali the great commentary (Mahabhashya).

14-003.r: Mudrarakshasa → Vishakhadatta; Gupta-period Sanskrit drama on how Chandragupta Maurya, helped by Kautilya, overthrew the Nandas.

14-005.r: All four are Gupta-era classics: Amarakosh (Amarsimha), Kamasutra (Vatsyayana), Meghaduta (Kalidasa), Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta).

14-006.r: Dashakumaracharitam → Dandin; Kumarasambhava → Kalidasa; Sursagar → Surdas; Ramcharitmanas, Vinaya Patrika → Tulsidas.

14-009.r: Janaki-haranam → Kumaradasa, not Kalidasa; Kalidasa wrote Malavikagnimitram, Abhigyan Shakuntalam, Kumarasambhavam.

14-010.r: Shringar Shatak → Bhartrihari (part of Shataka-traya), not Kalidasa; Kalidasa wrote Meghaduta (lyric) and Raghuvamsham (epic).

14-011.r: Uttararamacharitam → Bhavabhuti (play on Rama's later life), not Kalidasa; Kalidasa wrote Meghadutam, Kumarasambhavam, Ritusamharam.

14-012.r: 'Bible' of North Indian classical music → Natyashastra, Sanskrit treatise on performing arts by Bharat Muni.

14-013.r: Panini → Ashtadhyayi; Vatsyayana → Kamasutra; Chanakya → Arthashastra; Kalhana → Rajatarangini.

14-015.r: Kalhana's Rajatarangini ('River of Kings') → history of Kashmir; Ashtadhyayi → Panini.

14-017.r: Gaudavaho (Prakrit epic) → Vakpati, court poet of Yasovarman of Kanauj; describes Yasovarman's digvijaya.

14-018.r: Bharavi → Kiratarjuniyam; Harsha → Nagananda; Kalidasa → Malavikagnimitram; Rajasekhara → Karpuramanjari.

14-019.r: Kiratarjuniyam → Bharavi; epic on the fight of Arjuna and Shiva (disguised as a kirata hunter).

14-020.r: Mahabharata-based works: Naishadhiyacharita (Sriharsha; Nala-Damayanti), Kiratarjuniyam (Bharavi), Sisupalavadha (Magha); not Dashakumaracharita (Dandi; 10 princes).

14-021.r: Vishakhadatta → Drama; Varahamihira → Astronomy; Charaka → Medicine; Brahmagupta → Mathematics.

14-022.r: Charaka → Medicine; Brahmagupta → Mathematics; Varahamihira → Astrology; Vishakhadatta → Playwright.

14-023.r: Charaka Samhita → Medicine (Ayurveda); Charaka = father of Indian medicine.

14-024.r: Charaka Samhita (oldest surviving Ayurveda text) → 120 chapters in 8 sections.

14-025.r: Amarkosha → Amarsimha, not Varahamihira; Varahamihira wrote Panchasiddhantika, Brihat Samhita, Brihat Jataka.

14-026.r: Varahamihira's Panchasiddhantika → based on Greek astronomy (book adds Roman, Egyptian and Indian).

14-027.r: Nitisara, early book on politics → Kamandaka.

14-028.r: Wrong pair: Subandhu–Kadambari; Kadambari → Banabhatta. Correct: Kalidasa–Raghuvansa, Bhasa–Svapnavasavadattam, Harsha–Ratnavali.

14-029.r: Milindapanha → Pali text; dialogue between Buddhist monk Nagasena and Indo-Greek king Milinda (Menander).
14-029.h: Milinda + panha (questions) = King Menander's questions to Nagasena.

14-034.r: Text describing eight phases of agricultural work → Milindapanha (Pali; Nagasena–Menander dialogue).

14-035.r: Wrong pair: Khuman Raso–Karnidan; Khuman Raso → Dalpati Vijay. Correct: Prithviraj Raso–Chand Bardai; Bisaldeva Raso–Narapati; Shatrusal Raso–Dungar Singh.

14-036.r: Jaina texts → Parishishtaparvan (Hemchandra), Trishashtilakshana Mahapurana (Chamund Rai); Nettipakarana and Avadanashataka are Buddhist.

14-037.r: Court poets: Amir Khusrau → Alauddin Khalji; Kalidasa → Chandragupta II; Harisena → Samudragupta; Banabhatta → Harshavardhana.

14-038.r: Kalhana's contemporary ruler → Jai Singh (Jaisimha, 1128-1149) of Kashmir; Rajatarangini has 8 Tarangas and 7826 verses.

14-040.r: Kalhana's Rajatarangini (12th century) continued by Jonaraja (to Sultan Zainul Abedin's reign) and then his pupil Srivara.

14-042.h: Harsha's three plays: N-R-P, 'Naga Ratna Priya'.

14-045.r: Encyclopedic work → Brihat Samhita of Varahamihira (Gupta period).

14-046.r: Bhavabhuti, Hastimalla, Kshemeshvara → playwrights; Bhavabhuti, court poet of Yashovarman of Kannauj (Mahaviracharitam, Malatimadhava, Uttararamacharitam); Hastimalla, Kannada poet under Hoysalas.

14-047.r: Correct: Mrichchhakatikam–Sudraka, Mudrarakshasa–Vishakhadatta, Harshacharita–Banabhatta. Wrong: Buddhacharita is by Ashvaghosha, not Vasubandhu.

14-048.r: Only Kalidasa–Chandragupta II is right; Amarasimha was also in Chandragupta II's Navratna; Patanjali (not Panini) was with Pushyamitra Shunga.

14-049.r: Varahamihira → Brihat Samhita; Vishakhadatta → Devi-Chandraguptam; Sudraka → Mrichchhakatikam; Bilhana → Vikramankadevacharita; Prabandha Chintamani → Merutunga.

14-050.r: Two correct: Hammira Mahakavya–Nayachandra Suri; Nitivakyamrita–Somadeva Suri. Wrong: Devichandragupta → Vishakhadatta; Milinda-panha → Nagasena.

14-051.r: Parmar history sources: Navasahasankacharita (Padmagupta), Prabandha Chintamani (Merutunga), Udaipur Prashasti; Navasahasankacharita calls Mount Abu the Parmaras' origin.

14-052.r: Wrong pair: Karpuramanjari–Harsha; it is by Rajashekhara, poet laureate of the Gurjara-Pratiharas.

14-053.r: Shakuntalam → Kalidasa; his seven works: Abhigyanshakuntalam, Vikramorvashiyam, Malavikagnimitram, Raghuvamsham, Kumarasambhavam, Meghadutam, Ritusamharam.
14-053.h: 3 plays (Shakuntalam, Vikramorvashiyam, Malavikagnimitram), 2 epics (Raghu, Kumara), 2 lyrics (Megha, Ritu).

14-054.r: Mrichchhakatikam → Sudraka, not Kalidasa; Kalidasa wrote Meghaduta, Ritusamharam, Vikramorvashiyam.

14-055.r: Hero of Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram → Agnimitra, Shunga king of Vidisha (son of the Shunga founder); Kalidasa's first play, 5 acts.

14-058.r: Madhyama-vyayoga → Bhasa; Kavyalankara → Bhamaha; Natyashastra → Bharata Muni; Mahabhashya → Patanjali.

14-059.r: Gita Govinda → Jayadeva (twelfth century, Sanskrit), court poet of King Lakshman Sen of Bengal; twelve chapters.

14-061.r: Trivikrama Bhatta → Nala Champu; Somadeva → Kathasaritsagara; Jayadeva → Gita Govinda; Kshemendra → Brihatkathamanjari.

14-063.r: Ashtanga Samgraha → Medicine; Dasharupaka → Play (drama); Lilavati → Maths; Mahabhashya → Grammar.

14-064.r: 'Thy right is to work only, but never with its fruits' → Bhagavad Gita.

14-065.r: Source silent about ancient Indian trade routes (per book) → Sangam literature; Milindapanha and Jataka tales are not.

14-066.r: 'What is here is found elsewhere, but what is not here is found nowhere else' → Mahabharata.

14-067.r: Panchatantra (animal fables, Sanskrit) → by Vishnu Sharma; translated into 15 Indian and 40 (book: at least 50) foreign languages; Mughal version Ayar-e-Danish by Abul Fazl.

14-069.r: Ramacharitam → Sandhyakar Nandi; Navasahasankacharita → Padmagupta; Kumarapalacharita → Hemachandra; Vikramankadevacharita → Bilhana.

14-070.r: Sarvavarma → Katantra; Sudraka → Mrichchhakatikam; Vigyaneshwara → Mitakshara; Kalhana → Rajatarangini.

14-071.r: Devana Bhatta → Smriti Chandrika; Hemadri → Chaturvarga Chintamani; Madhvacharya → Parashar Madhav; Ballal Sena → Daan Sagar.

14-072.r: Mitakshara (Vijnanesvara): sons claim property in father's lifetime; Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana): only after his death. Both are inheritance laws, not caste-based codes.

14-073.r: Algebra → Bhaskara II (Bhaskaracharya, 12th century); his Siddhantasiromani has Lilavati (maths), Bijaganita (algebra), Ganitadhyaya, Goladhyaya.
14-073.t: Don't confuse Bhaskara II (Lilavati) with Bhaskara I or Aryabhatta.

14-076.r: Aryabhatta → mathematician and astronomer; wrote Aryabhatiya; said earth is spherical and rotates on its axis; father of trigonometry.

14-078.r: Mattavilasa Prahasana → Pallava ruler Mahendravarman I; depicts social and religious life.

14-080.r: Ancient name 'Nilotpala' for the Mahanadi → Vayu Purana.

14-081.r: Manusmriti (Manav Dharmashastra) → mainly the social system; one of 18 major Smritis; Manu = first law-giver of India.

14-084.r: Natyashastra → Bharatamuni; treatise on performing arts (drama, dance, music).

14-085.r: Zero → discovered by an anonymous Indian (second century B.C.); Arabs learnt it from India and spread it to Europe; Arab use from 873 A.D.

14-087.r: Wrong pair: The Natural History–Ptolemy; it is by Pliny the Elder (Roman). Correct: Life of Hiuen Tsang–Hui-li; Historiae Philippicae–Pompeius Trogus; The Histories–Herodotus.

14-088.r: Most ancient instrument → Veena; Sitar, Sarod and Tabla came in the medieval era.

15-001.r: Prithviraj Chauhan → Prithviraja III of Ajmer; beat Muhammad Ghori at First Tarain (1191 AD), lost Second Tarain (1192 AD).

15-002.r: Chauhan ruler of Ajmer who took Delhi → Vigraharaj IV; beat the Tomaras, seized Eastern Punjab and Delhi; most powerful Chauhan ruler.
15-002.t: Don't pick Prithviraj III; Delhi was already won by Vigraharaj IV.

15-003.r: Inscriptions show Bihar's rulers had contact with Java-Sumatra; Pala king Devapala ('Param Saugat') granted five villages at Sailendra king Balaputradeva's request for a Nalanda vihara.

15-004.r: Suvarnabhumi ruler who built a Nalanda monastery and asked Devapala for five villages → Balaputradeva (Sailendra).

15-005.r: Kumaradevi, Buddhist queen of Govind Chandra Gahadavala → built Dharma-Chakra-Jina Vihara at Sarnath.

15-006.r: Hammir Mahakavya calls the Chauhans Suryavanshi (descendants of Chahman, son of the Sun); one of the four fire (Agni) clans.

15-007.r: Alha-Udal → Mahoba; commanders of Chandel king Parmardidev (Parmal, 1165-1203 CE); Alha-Khand by Jagnik; Prithviraj Raso by Chand Bardai.

15-010.t: Don't confuse with Prithviraj Raso, which is by Chand Bardai.

15-011.r: Wrong pair: Abdur Rehman–Hammir Raso; Hammir Raso → Jodhraj. Correct: Chand Bardai–Prithviraj Raso; Jagnik–Alha-Khand; Narpati Nalh–Visal Dev Raso.

15-012.r: City of Dhillika (Delhi), eighth century → founded by Anangpal of the Tomar dynasty, once feudatories of the Gurjara-Pratiharas.

15-013.r: Jejakabhukti → ancient name of Bundelkhand; named after Jeja/Jejak (Jay Shakti), grandson of Chandel founder Nannuk.

15-014.r: Dhanga (Dangdev) → Chandela king of Jejakabhukti; gave up his body at the Ganga-Yamuna Sangam, Prayagraj.

15-015.r: Chandela order: Yashovarman (925-950 AD) → Dhanga (950-1002) → Vidyadhara (1017/19-1029) → Kirtivarman (1060-1100).

15-016.r: Tribhuvan Narayan (Samidheshwar) temple, Chittor → Paramara Raja Bhoj of Malwa; three-faced Shiva idol like Elephanta's.

15-017.r: Pundravardhana Bhukti → North Bengal; expanded beyond north Bihar under the Pala, Chandra and Sena dynasties.

15-018.r: Founder of the Pala dynasty → Gopala; per Lama Taranath, born near Pundravardhana and elected king of Bengal.

15-019.r: Odantapuri (Uddandapur) education centre → Bihar; founded by Pala ruler Gopala.

15-020.r: Somapura Mahavihara (Paharpur) and Vikramshila → built by Pala king Dharmapala ('Param Saugat'); Haribhadra in his court; founded 50 religious schools (Taranath).

15-021.r: Vikramshila University → founded by Dharmapala (770-810 A.D.) of Bengal; main Buddhist centre after Nalanda's decline.

15-022.r: Vikramshila University (Maha Vihar) → Dharmapala of the Pala dynasty; chief seat of Buddhist study after Nalanda declined.
15-022.t: Don't pick Gopala (Odantapuri) or Devapala (Nalanda grants); Vikramshila is Dharmapala's.

15-029.r: Vikramshila University → Bhagalpur, Bihar; founded by Pala ruler Dharmapala (770-810 AD).

15-030.r: Vikramshila: in Bhagalpur (not Banka); founded by Dharmapala (not Gopala I); Vajrayana flourished; astronomy, logic, law, grammar, philosophy also taught.

15-031.r: Kings chosen by the people → Gopala (Pala; Khalimpur inscription, to end Matsya Nyaya) and Nandivarman Pallavamalla (after Parameshvaravarman's death).

15-032.r: Not an early medieval learning centre → Taxila (early Buddhist centre, Gandhara capital, now Rawalpindi, Pakistan); Nalanda, Vikramshila, Uddantapur were.

15-033.r: Founder of the Rashtrakuta empire → Danti Durga (753 AD); performed the Hiranyagarbha ritual at Ujjayini.

15-035.r: Born in a military camp → Rashtrakuta Amoghavarsha I (800 AD, Shribhavan near Narmada), while father Govind III returned from North Indian campaigns.

15-036.r: Greatest Pratihara king → Mihir Bhoj (836-885 A.D.); Mahendrapala I Pratihara (885-910); Dharmapala = Pala; Harsha = Pushyabhuti.

15-037.r: Titles 'Adi Varaha' and 'Prabhas' → Gurjara-Pratihara Mihir Bhoja I, a Vaishnava and the most powerful Pratihara.

15-038.r: False: Mihir Bhoja was son of Nagabhatta II; he was son of Ramabhadra and Appa Devi. True: capital Kannauj (from c. 836 AD); Al-Masudi called him Baura.

15-039.r: Pratihara order: Vatsaraja (775-800 AD) → Nagabhatta II (800-833) → Mahendrapala I (885-910) → Mahipala (912-944).

15-040.r: Not a Gurjara-Pratihara → Bharatrabhatta I. Pratiharas (Ujjain, later Kannauj): Nagabhatta I (730-760), Vatsaraja, Nagabhatta II, Mihir Bhoja I, Mahendrapala I, Devapala (948-949).
15-040.t: This Devapala is a Pratihara king; don't confuse him with the Pala king Devapala.

15-041.r: Arab traveller Suleman visited India under Pratihara king Mihir Bhoja (Bhoja I).

15-042.r: Jain scholar Hemchandra → court of Solanki king Kumarapala (1143-1172 A.D.) as adviser; first rose to fame under Jaysimha Siddharaja.

15-043.r: Lakshmana Samvat (new era) → Sena king Lakshmanasena (1178-1206 A.D.; reigned 28 years).

15-045.r: Medieval jurists → Vigyaneshvara (Mitakshara), Hemadri, Jimutavahana (Dayabhaga); Rajashekhara was a poet in the Pratihara court, not a jurist.

15-046.r: Sena order: (Samantasena) → Hemanta Sena → Vijay Sena → Ballal Sena → Lakshmana Sena → (Vishvarupasena); father-to-son succession.

15-047.r: Rajashekhara → court of Pratihara Mahendrapala I and his son Mahipala I; wrote Karpuramanjari, Kavyamimamsa, Viddhasalabhanjika, Bal Ramayana; not Prabandhachintamani (Merutunga).

15-049.r: Capitals: Pratihara → Kannauj; Chola → Tanjore; Paramara → Dhara; Solanki → Anhilwada.

15-050.r: Two correct: Nannuka–Chandela; Nagabhata II–Gurjara Pratihara. Wrong: Jayashakti was Chandela (not Paramara); Bhoja was Paramara (not Rashtrakuta).

15-051.r: Founder of Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty → Nagabhatta I (730-760 AD); Agni-clan Rajputs; Gurjars first named in Pulakesin II's Aihole inscription and Harshacharita.

15-052.r: Tripartite struggle for Kannauj (8-9th century) → Pala, Gurjara-Pratihara, Rashtrakuta; Pratiharas won; Cholas were not part.
15-052.h: PPR: Pala (east), Pratihara (west), Rashtrakuta (south) fighting for Kannauj.

15-055.r: 'Nagar Mahodaya Shri' → Kannauj (name used under Mihir Bhoj).

15-056.r: Wrong pair: Jejakabhukti–Kaushambi; Jejakabhukti = Bundelkhand. Correct: Koil–Aligarh; Mahotsav Nagar–Mahoba; Mahodaya Shri–Kannauj.

15-057.r: Rashtrakuta Govind III (Dhruva's successor) defeated Pratihara Nagabhatta II; victory recorded in Sanjan and Radhanpur copper plates.

15-058.r: Aid to rebuild a demolished mosque at Khambhat → Chalukya king Jayasimha Siddharaja (per Muhammad Aufi; 1 lakh Balom).

15-059.r: Garhwal's Parmar (Panwar) dynasty → founded by Kanak Pal (Chandpur Garhi); Ajai Pal later united Garhwal. Malwa's Paramaras (capital Dhara) → founded by Upendra (Krishnaraja), 9th century AD.
15-059.c: The options are rulers of Garhwal's Parmar (Panwar) dynasty, founded by Kanak Pal, so the commission's key (b) is right. Upendra (Krishnaraja) founded the Malwa Paramaras of Dhara, which the book discusses instead.

15-060.r: King Bhoja (Paramara) → ruled from Dhara; early Paramara capital Ujjain, later moved to Dhara.
15-060.h: Scholars' lament on Bhoja's death: 'Adya Dhara Niradhara' (today Dhara is without support).

15-061.r: Samarangana Sutradhara (on mechanical/scientific devices) → Paramara king Bhoja; also wrote Saraswati Kanthabharan, Rajamartand, Yukti Kalpataru.
15-061.c: Book prints (a) Bhoja but notes the commission's revised key changed the answer to (b) Govindraja.

15-062.r: Udaipur Prashasti praises Paramara king Bhoja: did what no one else could; likened to Prithu; ruled from Kailash to the Malaya mountains.

15-063.r: Bhojshala (Dhar, M.P.) → presiding deity Goddess Saraswati; built by Paramara Bhoj in 1035 A.D. as a Sanskrit school; now in Kamal Maula Mosque premises.

15-064.r: Not a Paramara → Gangeyadeva (Kalachuri; took title Vikramaditya, revived gold coins); Upendra, Munj and Udayaditya were Paramaras.

15-065.r: Arab writer who described Kalachuri Gangeyadeva and his capital Tripuri → Al-Biruni (Tarikh al-Hind).

15-066.r: Correct: Khajuraho–Bundelkhand; Tirupati–Rayalaseema. Wrong: Bodhgaya is in Bihar; Shirdi and Nashik are in Maharashtra.

15-067.r: Gaudavaho → Vakpati, court poet of Yashovarman, king of Kannauj.

15-068.r: Araghatta → animal-driven waterwheel (Persian wheel) for irrigation; mentioned in Panchatantra and Rajatarangini.

15-069.r: 'Akbar of Kashmir' → Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (original name Shahi Khan; took throne 1420 A.D., ruled about 50 years); liberal religious policy, patron of learning.

15-071.r: Founder of Karnata dynasty → Nanyadev (1097-1147 AD); capital Simraungadh; ruled Mithila.

15-072.r: Last Karnata king → Harisimha (1295/1296-1324 AD); patron of art and literature; started the Panji system.

15-073.r: Kuruspal inscription (Bastar, Chhattisgarh) → king Someshwar (Someswardeva) of the Nagavamsa; records a village grant.
